title: How an Everyday Word in a Tool Schema Changes AI Agents' Searches While Every Call Stays Valid
description: We test whether an everyday word allowed as a tool value can change an AI agent's searches while every call stays valid. A traveller can call any place to stay a “hotel”, but a booking tool's type field separates hotel from guesthouse. Earlier work found that schema names change accuracy, and on MultiWOZ, a public booking corpus, this field has more errors than any other field for one dialogue tracker. However, that work did not measure exclusion of every fitting option, test schema updates or compare repairs. At the traveller's first mention of “hotel”, 5.6% to 18.8% of seven models' valid answers would have excluded every venue fitting the recorded task. In two tests registered before we opened the answers, we renamed type: hotel to property_kind: large_property. Counting large_property as hotel, the share of answers with a hotel value fell by 13.0 percentage points where the task sets no type, and by 29.1 points where the task's first or final choice is a hotel. Exploratory tool-text rewrites, made after a commission statement and a request to favour one type, raised one agent's exclusions by about 19 points. An exploratory release test of old against new schemas flagged the rename on all five models. It flagged 0 of 9 decisions on unchanged or reordered schemas and 2 of 7 on paraphrases, and neither flag recurred. Against corpus labels, all four planned repairs failed a rule, fixed beforehand, for removing extra values without losing too many needed values (exploratory). Against the traveller's explicit words, a verifier that asks the model whether the traveller excludes guesthouses passed on 5 of 9 models (post hoc), but this reference asks nearly the verifier's question. A symbolic database rule, with no model call, avoided about as many displays with no fitting venue as the verifier (post hoc). Builders should therefore measure exclusion, test schema updates before release and set references before repair tests. The evidence concerns one word in one corpus.
